# Good workflows {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## What is a good AI workflow

A good AI workflow for bioinformatics largely replicates a good bioinformatics workflow. As with how we code more traditionally, taking short-cuts comes back to haunt us later. Very little of Bioinformatics is just 'plug and play'.

Key cornerstones:

- Planning
- Reproducibility
- Checkpoints and Review

## Getting Started

Open up Claude Code or OpenAI Codex and start a new project. 

The folder you provide will define the scope. This means where on your computer it will have access to. You will also want to add any files there you want it to be able to read. 

?Add screenshot exmaple?

# Planning {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Planning

To start with we need do make decisions about how we will address our problem.

For example:

"I have some scRNAseq data from mouse fat cells. I want to do some generate clusters of fat cell sub types"

At this point you can decide what software to use (Seurat/Scanpy) and what reference to use (mm10/mm39). 

Having a plan is important from the outset. If you are unfamiliar with the analysis the broad-stroked planning is the opportunity to start understanding what are the conceptual steps in the analysis. That way you can keep your hands on the wheel.

## Planning

Working collaboratively with the LLMs to make an analysis plan document is a good place to start. This will help break down your broad objectives into smaller tasks. This will also provide a backbone which will handover between analysis sessions.

"I have some scRNAseq data from mouse fat cells. I want to do some generate clusters of fat cell sub types. I want help building an analysis workflow. First though we will work together to make key decisions like software and which analysis steps are required. In the process I want to make an analysis plan document broken down into the key steps for the workflow"

?link to example plan?

## Planning

You can use LLMs to help with planning, but as always, do not take it purely at face value. Validate with trusted sources. Remember the context of your experiment is everything and tools can be fickle. 

It is ultimately up to you to decide what is the best approach.

i.e. scRNAseq has a pretty standard QC workflow, but there are many edge cases:
- Cell cycle regression can have negative consequences for Neurons
- Standard filters will vary between snRNA and scRNAseq
- Relaxed filtering may be necessary to detect rare cell types

# Reproducibility {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Reproducibility

LLMs in general are not reproducible. If I ask the same prompt multiple times I will get different response as the context evolves. 

Even if someone trying to replicate my work was able to match the context identically they would also need to use the identical model. Frontier models like those from Claude and ChatGPT though are dynamic, update, and are then retired with limited to access them. 

If this is the state of play how do you stay reproducible?


? try to show example of same prompts twice?

## Reproducibility

There are two aspects that are most important to ensure that you stay reproducible.

* Manage and save your software versions
* Always make code

The LLMs should not be covertly running code and making plots without it also saving that code and saving how or where this was ran. This is the most important step that we see skipped by people doing their own LLM-supported analysis.

## Managing software

It doesn't matter if you are running code in R, python, shell scripts etc. What matters is that you have static versions of these software and the packages they use across your analysis. This means once you start on a project you do not update the software. 

You can use package managers like Conda/Mamba or create containers like Dockers to help manage your software and also enable you to share these with other people or other systems i.e. HPC. 

You do not need to do this alone though. Setting up these software environments is something that Claude and ChatGPT are pretty good at. Once you are set up you can ensure it takes an appropriate snapshot, then you are good to go. 

?Show diagram of how these fit together?
? Show an example prompt?

## Always make code

Once you have your software the next step is code. You can easily prompt code generation by simply asking for it.

Especially when working on my laptop I will have a folder in which I will have data, results and the code which links the two. 

If we are using an Claude Code or Codex, these files will be generated in your project. 

Ideally you would be using Git and Github as you go to mange version control. Again Claude can help with this. 

# Checkpoints and Review {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Checkpoints

As we mentioned with strengths and limitation we don't necessarily want to do everything at once for two main reasons:
  * Its easier for the LLMs to get overwhelmed by the scale of the task.
  * Its easier for the user to skip essential checkpoints and tests. 

? example prompt?

## Checkpoints

If you are trying something for the first time or working on something exploratory this is even more important. The key part is to do this piece-by-piece and review the outcomes. You should hopefully have technical and biological expectations about the data as it is processed

For example:
  * What distribution should the data have?
  * Should it be logged?
  * Should a marker gene be expressed in one sample and not the other?

## What should I do if I can't read the code

If you do not understand the code that you are generating take some extra time and break it down. Just because it runs, does not mean it is doing what you want it to do. 

These steps are based on key principles in Bioinformatics that we use when we run new tools or languages we are unfamiliar with. 

* **Ask for annotation of the code** - Once annotated read the overviews and ask questions (not just to the LLMs). Add your own additional annotations to help fill in the gaps.

* **Run it** - If code is wrong, it often errors or gives warnings. If it runs, check the output is right. If you don't know what right looks like then you need some positive controls and trial datasets. If it gives warnings, double-check why. 

* **Look it up** - Check arguments against the package help and vignettes. Check anytime it points you to a paper. Review the core principles of your analysis

## What should I do if I can't read the code 

* **Start small** - Only use a small amount of the data. You do not need to run all the data at once. Make sure you understand it first so you know it is doing what is is supposed to be doing. 

* **Double-check what it is actually doing** - As you work through chunks of code, check the saved variables. Do they look as expected? If not, why?

* **Verify the numbers** - Does it make sense? Export results to spreadsheets so you can manually review. Do directions of changes make sense? Does the normalization make sense? Compare to plots and visualizations.

- **Cross-check** - Ask in a fresh session, or a different model, and compare. Disagreement means look carefully. You can also ask it to perform an This is *Adversarial Review* of the code that has been generated. 

You remain responsible for everything the tool produces (see *Journal policies* in the LLM Basics section).



# Other things to consider {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}

## Mananging resources

When you are building scripts and planning something that is a little more computationally intensive you should also consider the resources you have available to you. Either on your laptop or on remote servers i.e. HPC systems. 

Already we suggest running your analysis on a subset to start, so you can make sure the code itself runs ok.

Once you have functioning code and are ready to run everything, then you should provide information about your computational setup so LLMs can adapt the code to your limits. 

## Building Reports

We work with reports as the hub for our deliverable analysis. Reports enable us to tie code directly to our output figures in fixed documents. This means no orphan plots where we're not sure exactly how they were generated. 

Popular examples include Quarto, Rmarkdown and Jupyter.


## Good practice still applies

To summarize, even when we have LLM-assisted coding, good coding practice is still essential. If you lean on vibe-coding an analysis it opens the door to mistakes. 

- Planning
- Reproducibility
- Checkpoints and Review


# Hard lines {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle}


## Why rules loosen over time

As we give more capabilities and autonomy to the LLMs we will then want to know how we define limits.  

Many of us may have data that we do not want shared with LLMs and/or files that we want to protect from Agents i.e. personal data, raw files, logins etc.
